title: Extreme Weather and Attribution
objective: After this level you can explain how warming shifts the odds of heat waves and downpours and how scientists test a single event.
summary: Warming has made heatwaves and downpours more frequent and intense. Attribution studies compare today's climate with one without human influence; tornado links remain uncertain.

cards.headline: Scientists don't ask if warming caused a storm. They ask a sharper question.
cards.body: How much more likely, or how much stronger, did warming make it? That question has answers, and for some kinds of weather the answer is very clear.

cards.headline: Loaded dice
cards.body: The IPCC finds it virtually certain that heatwaves and other hot extremes have become more frequent and more intense over most land since the 1950s, with human-caused warming the main driver. Heavy downpours have increased too. Part of the reason is from Level 85: for every 1 °C of warming, the air can hold about 7 percent more water vapor, so storms have more water to drop.

cards.headline: Testing one event
cards.body: To test a single event, scientists run computer models twice: once for today's climate and once with the human influence removed. Comparing them shows how much more likely or intense the event became. For the record July 2019 heatwave in France and the Netherlands, World Weather Attribution found climate change made it at least 10 times more likely.

cards.headline: Not every extreme is the same
cards.body: The evidence is strongest for heat and heavy rain. For tornadoes, scientists have low confidence in any link to climate change so far: tornadoes are small and short-lived, which makes them very hard to model. Good science says "we know" where it knows, and "not yet" where it doesn't.

mascot.line: People mix this up: attribution doesn't say warming caused a storm. It measures how much warming loaded the dice.

cards.headline: Extremes and attribution: tested
learned: Heatwaves are more frequent and intense

questions.prompt: So far, scientists have low confidence in a link between climate change and _____.

options.label: heatwaves
options.rationale: The link to heat is strong.

options.label: heavy downpours
options.rationale: Heavy rain has increased, likely driven by human warming.

questions.explanation: Tornadoes are small and short-lived, so their link to climate change is still uncertain.

questions.prompt: Match each kind of extreme weather with what the evidence says.
questions.explanation: It is virtually certain heatwaves have become more frequent and intense, heavy downpours have increased too, and scientists have low confidence in any tornado link so far.

questions.prompt: Plants like an oak release water vapor into the air. In a warmer world the air can hold more of it. What follows for rainstorms?

options.label: They have more water available to drop
They become rarer, since vapor stays aloft forever
They lose their water back to the trees
options.rationale: The added vapor feeds the storms.

options.label: Nothing, since vapor isn't part of the water cycle
options.rationale: Water vapor is part of the hydrosphere and the water cycle.

questions.explanation: Warmer air holds about 7 percent more vapor per 1 °C, giving storms more water for heavy downpours.
